Data Partitioning

1. What is Data Partitioning?
  • Data partitioning divides the entire dataset into smaller chunks called partitions;
  • Partitions are distributed across server nodes so each node holds roughly an equal share of data;
  • By default each cache has 1024 partitions;
  • This is how Ignite scales horizontally — more nodes means each node stores fewer partitions;
2. How Keys Map to Partitions
  • When you write a key-value pair, Ignite applies the affinity function to the key to determine the partition number (0–1023);
  • The default affinity function uses a rendezvous hashing algorithm;
  • The partition is then assigned to a primary node and optionally to backup nodes;
  • Key "user-42"  →  hash("user-42") mod 1024  →  Partition 317  →  Node B (primary)
                                                                     →  Node D (backup)
3. Partitioned vs. Replicated Mode
Mode Description Reads Writes Best For
PARTITIONED Data is split across nodes; each node holds a subset May require network hop Fast (update primary + backups) Large datasets with frequent writes
REPLICATED Every node holds a full copy of all data Always local (fast) Slow (must update all nodes) Small, read-heavy lookup tables
LOCAL Data stays on the node that created it; no distribution Local only Local only Node-local caching, scratch space
4. Backup Partitions
  • Each partition has exactly one primary copy and zero or more backup copies;
  • Backups are stored on different nodes from the primary for fault tolerance;
  • If the primary node fails, a backup is automatically promoted to primary;
  • Number of backups is configured per cache: 
    CacheConfiguration cacheCfg = new CacheConfiguration("myCache");
cacheCfg.setBackups(2); // 1 primary + 2 backups = 3 copies total
  • Trade-off: more backups = better fault tolerance but more memory usage and slower writes;
5. Partition Loss Policy
  • If both the primary and all backup nodes for a partition fail simultaneously, the partition is lost;
  • The partitionLossPolicy controls what happens:
    • READ_ONLY_SAFE — lost partitions become read-only; reads from non-lost partitions continue;
    • READ_ONLY_ALL — all partitions become read-only;
    • READ_WRITE_SAFE — lost partitions throw exceptions; others continue normally;
    • READ_WRITE_ALL — all operations continue (may return incomplete data);
    • IGNORE (default) — partition loss is ignored;
